extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians of economic thought
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of how the monopoly of the colony trade and mercantile regulations affect capital allocation, productive labour, prices, profits, and the overall political economy of a country (Adam Smith's argument). Useful as a set of normative principles for evaluating trade/mercantile policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly raises domestic prices and reduces consumption and production
rubrics_metrics.description: Use, in such branches of trade, her merchants cannot get this greater profit without selling dearer than they otherwise would do, both the goods of foreign countries which they import into their own, and the goods of their own country which they export to foreign countries. Their own country must both buy dearer and sell dearer; must both buy less, and sell less; must both enjoy less and produce less, than she otherwise would do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that monopoly-induced higher merchant profits are realized through higher prices, which reduce both domestic enjoyment (consumption) and production. This is a general criterion for judging monopoly effects on national welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly creates relative disadvantage vs countries without the same disadvantage
rubrics_metrics.description: It subjects her to a relative disadvantage; because, in such branches of trade, it sets other countries, which are not subject to the same absolute disadvantage, either more above her or less below her, than they otherwise would be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopoly can make a country relatively worse off in certain branches by enabling foreign competitors to enjoy and produce more; use this to evaluate international competitiveness effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: High profits of stock can raise prices as much as high wages
rubrics_metrics.description: The high profits of British stock, however, may contribute towards raising the price of British manufactures, in many cases, as much, and in some perhaps more, than the high wages of British labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing causes of high prices and loss of export competitiveness, consider both wages and profits of stock; merchants may overlook their own role in price increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly draws and drives capital away from non-monopoly branches
rubrics_metrics.description: It has partly been drawn from those branches of trade, by the attraction of superior profit in the colony trade... It has partly been driven from them, by the advantage which the high rate of profit established in Great Britain gives to other countries, in all the different branches of trade of which Great Britain has not the monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopoly reallocates capital toward privileged trades and away from other sectors, altering domestic industry composition — a criterion for assessing structural distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly reduces competition of domestic capital and increases foreign competition
rubrics_metrics.description: In those other branches of trade, it has diminished the competition of British capitals, and thereby raised the rate of British profit higher than it otherwise would have been. On the contrary, it has increased the competition of foreign capitals, and thereby sunk the rate of foreign profit lower than it otherwise would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how monopoly changes competitive dynamics domestically and abroad and how that affects profit rates in different countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment value of capital depends on frequency of returns
rubrics_metrics.description: The most advantageous employment of any capital to the country to which it belongs, is that which maintains there the greatest quantity of productive labour... the quantity of productive labour which any capital employed in the foreign trade of consumption can maintain, is exactly in proportion ... to the frequency of its returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating forms of foreign trade, measure advantage by how frequently capital returns to sustain productive labour — frequent returns support more productive labour per unit of capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colony trade often forces capital into more distant, less frequent-return trades
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly of the colony trade has, in all cases, forced some part of the capital of Great Britain from a foreign trade of consumption carried on with a neighbouring, to one carried on with a more distant country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that privileging distant colony trade reduces turnover frequency and thus the productive labour sustained by that capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round-about trade (re-exporting via domestic port) reduces effective employment of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: That part of the capital of Great Britain which brings those eighty-two thousand hogsheads to Great Britain, which re-exports them from thence to those other countries... is employed in a round-about foreign trade of consumption; and is necessarily forced into this employment, in order to dispose of this great surplus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round-about trade adds delays (longer return cycles) and requires larger capital for same employment — evaluate trade structures for directness and turnover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly can convert consumption trade into carrying trade, supporting foreign industry
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly of the colony trade, therefore, so far as it has turned towards that trade a greater proportion of the capital of Great Britain than what would otherwise have gone to it, has in all cases turned it, from a foreign trade of consumption... into a carrying trade; and, consequently from supporting more or less the industry of Great Britain, to be employed altogether in supporting partly that of the colonies, and partly that of some other countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to judge whether a privileged trade primarily benefits the domestic economy or, via re-exports and carrying, sustains foreign producers instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly breaks natural balance among industry branches and increases systemic risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly of the colony trade... seems to have broken altogether that natural balance which would otherwise have taken place among all the different branches of British industry... the whole system of her industry and commerce has thereby been rendered less secure; the whole state of her body politic less healthful than it otherwise would have been.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concentration effects: specialization toward a single market increases vulnerability to shocks and political disorder; diversity across markets is healthier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual relaxation preferred to sudden opening of monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: Some moderate and gradual relaxation of the laws which give to Great Britain the exclusive trade to the colonies, till it is rendered in a great measure free, seems to be the only expedient which can, in all future times, deliver her from this danger... To open the colony trade all at once to all nations, might not only occasion some transitory inconveniency, but a great permanent loss, to the greater part of those whose industry or capital is at present engaged in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy change should be phased to avoid severe transitional harm; use staged removal of restraints to reallocate capital without catastrophic disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish colony trade effects from monopoly effects
rubrics_metrics.description: We must carefully distinguish between the effects of the colony trade and those of the monopoly of that trade. The former are always and necessarily beneficial; the latter always and necessarily hurtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the underlying economic activity (colony trade) separately from the institutional restriction (monopoly); free competition in the same trade yields different outcomes than monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free colony trade expands markets without diverting existing markets or capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of the colony trade, in its natural and free state, is to open a great though distant market... In its natural and free state, the colony trade, without drawing from those markets any part of the produce which had ever been sent to them, encourages Great Britain to increase the surplus continually...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free competition in new markets creates additional produce and capital rather than merely shifting existing produce; consider whether a trade policy creates net new activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly excludes foreign competition, raising profit rates and drawing capital/produce from old markets
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly of the colony trade, on the contrary, by excluding the competition of other nations, and thereby raising the rate of profit, both in the new market and in the new employment, draws produce from the old market, and capital from the old employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a monopoly, test whether it simply reallocates activity rather than producing additional national benefit; elevated profit rates signal distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly discourages improvement of land and retards rent and land price growth
rubrics_metrics.description: By raising the rate of mercantile profit, the monopoly discourages the improvement of land... the monopoly necessarily retards the natural increase of another great original source of revenue, the rent of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare returns to mercantile vs. agricultural improvement; policies that raise mercantile returns relative to improvement returns will divert capital away from land improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly raises market rate of interest and hurts landlords
rubrics_metrics.description: By raising the rate of profit, too, the monopoly necessarily keeps up the market rate of interest higher than it otherwise would be... The monopoly, therefore, hurts the interest of the landlord two different ways...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider knock-on effects of higher profit rates on interest and asset prices; landlords lose both slower rent growth and lower land price multiples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly reduces aggregate accumulation and total revenue despite higher merchant profit rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The monopoly raises the rate of profit, but it hinders the sum of profit from rising so high as it otherwise would do... The monopoly, by hindering it from affording so great a revenue as it would otherwise afford, necessarily hinders it from increasing so fast as it would otherwise increase...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess long-run effects on capital accumulation: high rates on smaller capital may produce less aggregate revenue than modest rates on larger capital (small profit on great capital > great profit on small capital).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly harms all original sources of revenue (wages, rent, profits) and thus national interest
rubrics_metrics.description: All the original sources of revenue, the wages of labour, the rent of land, and the profits of stock, the monopoly renders much less abundant than they otherwise would be. To promote the little interest of one little order of men in one country, it hurts the interest of all other orders of men in that country, and of all the men in all other countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this comprehensive welfare criterion to judge whether a policy that benefits a narrow class is detrimental to wider societal prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: High mercantile profits foster luxury and reduce parsimony, harming accumulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The high rate of profit seems everywhere to destroy that parsimony which, in other circumstances, is natural to the character of the merchant... Accumulation is thus prevented in the hands of all those who are naturally the most disposed to accumulate...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate behavioral effects of elevated profits on saving/consumption patterns of merchants and how that influences national capital formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other distortions (improper taxes, bad administration of justice, currency issues) amplify monopoly harms
rubrics_metrics.description: These causes seem to be other monopolies of different kinds: the degradation of the value of gold and silver... the exclusion from foreign markets by improper taxes upon exportation, and the narrowing of the home market, by still more improper taxes upon the transportation of goods... above all, that irregular and partial administration of justice which often protects the rich and powerful debtor...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing poor industrial outcomes, examine combined institutional distortions (taxes, currency, legal system) as compounding monopoly effects; examples: Spain and Portugal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural good effects of colony trade can outweigh monopoly harms given supportive institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In England, on the contrary, the natural good effects of the colony trade, assisted by other causes, have in a great measure conquered the bad effects of the monopoly... the general liberty of trade... the unbounded liberty of transporting them from one part of our own country to any other... above all, that equal and impartial administration of justice...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess net effects of a trade with monopoly by considering complementary institutions (domestic trade freedom, impartial justice) that can mitigate harm; institutional context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly alters the quality and direction of manufactures rather than increasing their quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the manufactures of Great Britain, however, have been advanced, as they certainly have, by the colony trade, it has not been by means of the monopoly of that trade, but in spite of the monopoly. The effect of the monopoly has been, not to augment the quantity, but to alter the quality and shape of a part of the manufactures of Great Britain...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between quantitative growth and qualitative reorientation of industry when evaluating policy impacts; monopoly may skew products toward markets with slow returns even if overall manufacturing appears to expand.
